Reference: Hsiao (2025)

Model Setting

The paper studies how government flood defense complicates long-run adaptation to sea level rise by creating coastal moral hazard. Jakarta, a megacity of 32 million residents on a delta where thirteen rivers meet the sea, already suffers about 300 million dollars of flood damages per year. Global sea level rise combines with land subsidence of 7 to 14 cm per year, driven by groundwater extraction, and official plans describe 3 to 5 m of relative sea level rise by 2050. The government has responded with a proposed sea wall costing up to 60 billion dollars and with a new political capital, Nusantara. The core argument is a commitment problem in the spirit of Kydland and Prescott (1977): the government would prefer ex ante not to protect coastal development, but once development is sunk it is ex post optimal to protect it, so developers over-build at the coast and force defense. The result is coastal lock-in that delays inland migration. The paper has three parts: a theory of development and defense based on monotone comparative statics; reduced-form evidence that development responds to defense; and a dynamic spatial model that combines static residential location choice, forward-looking developers who make sunk investments in immobile buildings, and a machine-learning hydrological model of flooding, used to compare commitment regimes and complementary policies. Data are compiled by 300 m cell (5,780 cells): building construction and population from the Global Human Settlement Layer, property prices from listings and transactions, land prices from the Jakarta Smart City appraisal data, and monthly tract-level flooding for 2013-2020.

Theory: Development and Defense

In a stylized example, a sea wall has public cost e>0e>0e>0, and a unit mass of small, identical developers can build at cost c>0c>0c>0. Behind a wall, buildings rent for r=c+ϵr=c+\epsilonr=c+ϵ and yield a small profit ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0; without a wall, flooded buildings cannot be rented and nobody builds. If r>e>ϵr>e>\epsilonr>e>ϵ, the government prefers ex ante not to build the wall, since profits ϵ<e\epsilon<eϵ<e do not justify it, but ex post, with construction costs sunk, it builds the wall because protected revenues satisfy r>er>er>e. With commitment the outcome is no wall, no coastal development, and zero welfare (the first best); without commitment developers force a wall and welfare is negative.

The general model considers one flood-prone coastal location. Development ddd and defense ggg generate private profits π(d,g)\pi(d,g)π(d,g) (consumer surplus of residents plus producer surplus of developers) at public cost e(d,g)e(d,g)e(d,g) (infrastructure for flood defense plus aid for flooded development). Social welfare is:

w(d,g)=π(d,g)−e(d,g)(9.2.2.1)w(d,g)=\pi(d,g)-e(d,g) \tag{9.2.2.1}w(d,g)=π(d,g)−e(d,g)(9.2.2.1)

Both π\piπ and eee are increasing in ddd and in ggg. Development and defense are complements: π\piπ has increasing differences in (d,g)(d,g)(d,g) because defense protects new buildings, and eee has decreasing differences because defense reduces the need for post-disaster aid. The timeline has three stages: the government announces a plan, developers build, and the government provides defense. Development maximizes private profits under perfect competition, and defense maximizes social welfare. The first best (d^∗,g^∗)(\hat{d}^*,\hat{g}^*)(d^∗,g^​∗) jointly maximizes social welfare, with d^∗=d∗(g^∗)\hat{d}^*=d^*(\hat{g}^*)d^∗=d∗(g^​∗) and g^∗=g∗(d^∗)\hat{g}^*=g^*(\hat{d}^*)g^​∗=g∗(d^∗):

d∗(g)=arg⁡max⁡d{w(d,g)},g∗(d)=arg⁡max⁡g{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.2)d^*(g)=\arg\max_{d}\left\{w(d,g)\right\},\qquad g^*(d)=\arg\max_{g}\left\{w(d,g)\right\} \tag{9.2.2.2}d∗(g)=argdmax​{w(d,g)},g∗(d)=arggmax​{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.2)

Theory: Moral Hazard and Commitment

Developers do not internalize public costs, and a time-inconsistent government responds to over-development with over-defense. The paper compares four regimes. Under strong commitment, the government commits to regulating development: a tax τ=e(d,g)\tau=e(d,g)τ=e(d,g) makes developers internalize public costs, so the equilibrium (d^C,g^C)(\hat{d}^C,\hat{g}^C)(d^C,g^​C) solves the same conditions as the first best. This is hard to sustain because, once development is sunk, the tax is a pure transfer that invites lobbying. Under weak commitment, the government commits only to limited defense and development responds to it:

dc(g)=arg⁡max⁡d{π(d,g)},g^c=arg⁡max⁡g{w(dc(g),g)}(9.2.2.3)d^c(g)=\arg\max_{d}\left\{\pi(d,g)\right\},\qquad \hat{g}^c=\arg\max_{g}\left\{w(d^c(g),g)\right\} \tag{9.2.2.3}dc(g)=argdmax​{π(d,g)},g^​c=arggmax​{w(dc(g),g)}(9.2.2.3)

with d^c=dc(g^c)\hat{d}^c=d^c(\hat{g}^c)d^c=dc(g^​c). Under weak non-commitment, the announcement is not credible, and defense responds to development:

dn(g)=arg⁡max⁡d{π(d,g)},gn(d)=arg⁡max⁡g{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.4)d^n(g)=\arg\max_{d}\left\{\pi(d,g)\right\},\qquad g^n(d)=\arg\max_{g}\left\{w(d,g)\right\} \tag{9.2.2.4}dn(g)=argdmax​{π(d,g)},gn(d)=arggmax​{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.4)

with d^n=dn(g^n)\hat{d}^n=d^n(\hat{g}^n)d^n=dn(g^​n) and g^n=gn(d^n)\hat{g}^n=g^n(\hat{d}^n)g^​n=gn(d^n). Under strong non-commitment, a current government (or a local government, or a developer association) chooses aggregate development to maximize private profits, anticipating that a future government will defend whatever has been built:

d^N=arg⁡max⁡d{π(d,gN(d))},gN(d)=arg⁡max⁡g{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.5)\hat{d}^N=\arg\max_{d}\left\{\pi(d,g^N(d))\right\},\qquad g^N(d)=\arg\max_{g}\left\{w(d,g)\right\} \tag{9.2.2.5}d^N=argdmax​{π(d,gN(d))},gN(d)=arggmax​{w(d,g)}(9.2.2.5)

with g^N=gN(d^N)\hat{g}^N=g^N(\hat{d}^N)g^​N=gN(d^N). The regimes are ranked with a generalized objective that puts weight 1−θ1-\theta1−θ on public costs:

w~(d,g,θ)=π(d,g)−(1−θ)e(d,g)(9.2.2.6)\tilde{w}(d,g,\theta)=\pi(d,g)-(1-\theta)e(d,g) \tag{9.2.2.6}w~(d,g,θ)=π(d,g)−(1−θ)e(d,g)(9.2.2.6)

Let the development problem use weight θd\theta_dθd​ and the defense problem use weight θg\theta_gθg​. Because w~\tilde{w}w~ has increasing differences in (d,g)(d,g)(d,g), (d,θ)(d,\theta)(d,θ) and (g,θ)(g,\theta)(g,θ), Topkis's theorem implies that best responses increase in the other action and in θ\thetaθ, Tarski's theorem gives existence of fixed points, and Milgrom and Roberts (1994) imply that the extreme fixed points increase in θd\theta_dθd​ and θg\theta_gθg​. The first best is (θd,θg)=(0,0)(\theta_d,\theta_g)=(0,0)(θd​,θg​)=(0,0), weak non-commitment is (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), and joint private-profit maximization is (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). Propositions 1 to 4 deliver the ranking:

d^N>d^n>d^c>d^∗=d^C,g^N>g^n>g^c>g^∗=g^C(9.2.2.7)\hat{d}^N>\hat{d}^n>\hat{d}^c>\hat{d}^*=\hat{d}^C,\qquad \hat{g}^N>\hat{g}^n>\hat{g}^c>\hat{g}^*=\hat{g}^C \tag{9.2.2.7}d^N>d^n>d^c>d^∗=d^C,g^​N>g^​n>g^​c>g^​∗=g^​C(9.2.2.7)

Less commitment means more coastal entrenchment: over-development and over-defense. Unlike moral hazard in insurance, the friction is time inconsistency rather than hidden action, and it is amplified by a feedback loop in which defense encourages development that forces more defense. Moral hazard vanishes if defense is infeasible, if defense is costless, or if there is no private adaptation to crowd out. Appendix extensions show that coastal entrenchment crowds out inland development and that public defense crowds out private defense.

Reduced-Form Evidence

The West Flood Canal, completed in 1918, diverts a major river around the city center and protects areas to its north but not to its south. Using eight digitized Dutch colonial maps (1887-1945) and a spatial regression discontinuity at the canal with 100 m cells and an optimal bandwidth of 500 m, the paper finds no robust discontinuity in land development before the canal (interaction coefficients between −0.09-0.09−0.09 and −0.00-0.00−0.00) and a jump to the north afterwards that grows from 0.31 in 1920 to 0.74 in 1945. Elevation is smooth at the boundary and modern flooding is lower to the north. Defense therefore encourages development.

Demand is estimated on the 2015 population distribution. Equilibrium

Rents clear the market for floor space in every location and period. Risk-neutral, competitive real estate investment trusts stand ready to buy developed and empty plots, so prices make landowners indifferent between selling and holding:

Complete arbitrage yields pricing equations:

pkt1=∑t′=1∞βt′E[rkt+t′],pkt0=βαln⁡(exp⁡(E[V^kt+11])+exp⁡(E[V~kt+10]))(9.2.2.18)p^1_{kt}=\sum_{t'=1}^{\infty}\beta^{t'}\mathbb{E}\left[r_{kt+t'}\right],\qquad p^0_{kt}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\ln\left(\exp\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{V}^1_{kt+1}\right]\right)+\exp\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{V}^0_{kt+1}\right]\right)\right) \tag{9.2.2.18}pkt1​=t′=1∑∞​βt′E[rkt+t′​],pkt0​=αβ​ln(exp(E[V^kt+11​])+exp(E[V~kt+10​]))(9.2.2.18)

Property prices are the net present value of rents, and land prices are the option value of development. Flooding lowers residential demand, hence rents, hence both prices; defense does the opposite.

Unobserved costs affect supply and therefore prices, so hkt2h_{kt}^2hkt2​ and pkt0p^0_{kt}pkt0​ are instrumented with residential amenities (proximity to schools, clinics and rail stations) as demand shifters. The approach requires only one cross-section, is agnostic about expectations of future flooding and defense (which are capitalized into prices, so that prices are a sufficient statistic for the incentive to develop), and assumes efficient markets and price-taking developers (Jakarta records 14,505 construction companies in 2021). An appendix derives an alternative Euler conditional-choice-probability equation in the style of Scott (2013), which needs two periods and rational expectations.

Flooding and the Sea Wall

Benefits of defense come from a hydrological model trained on monthly tract-level flooding for 2013-2020, with rainfall, elevation, slope, and distances to major rivers, minor rivers and the coast as inputs. A histogram gradient boosting decision tree with monotonicity constraints on elevation and distance to major rivers fits best (cross-validated R-squared of 0.471 against 0.027 for linear regression). A sea wall of height ggg is simulated by raising the elevation of the city uniformly by ggg; sea level rise lowers elevation uniformly (IPCC central projections of 0.20 m by 2050, 0.56 m by 2100 and 0.92 m by 2150), and land subsidence lowers it heterogeneously (projections of Andreas et al. (2018), above 5 m in some northern neighborhoods). Costs come from engineering estimates for the planned wall: 60 km onshore with 4 m of height and 32 km offshore with 24 m of height (8 m above water), at 11 billion dollars including maintenance that adds 35 percent in present value. Assuming costs linear in height and length, with offshore above-water height twice the onshore height, the cost in million dollars of a wall of height ggg meters is:

e(g)=10.67×60×g+10.78×32×(2g+16)(9.2.2.21)e(g)=10.67\times 60\times g+10.78\times 32\times(2g+16) \tag{9.2.2.21}e(g)=10.67×60×g+10.78×32×(2g+16)(9.2.2.21)

which gives 9.5 and 12 billion dollars for 3 m and 5 m walls. Because only direct sea wall costs are measured (not disaster aid or the opportunity cost of public funds), e(d,g)=e(g)e(d,g)=e(g)e(d,g)=e(g); strong commitment, weak commitment and weak non-commitment then coincide, and the quantitative analysis contrasts strong commitment with strong non-commitment.

Government Problem and Solution

With KKK locations in one period, defense maximizes the sum of location welfare wkw_kwk​, and development either takes defense as fixed (commitment) or anticipates the response of defense (non-commitment):

g∗(d)=arg⁡max⁡g{∑kwk(g;d)}d∗(g)=arg⁡max⁡d{∑kπk(d;g)}={dk∣Pkres(d;g)=Pkdev(dk)}dN=arg⁡max⁡d{∑kπk(d,g∗(d))}(9.2.2.22)\begin{aligned} g^*(d)&=\arg\max_{g}\left\{\sum_{k}w_k(g;d)\right\}\\ d^*(g)&=\arg\max_{d}\left\{\sum_{k}\pi_k(d;g)\right\}=\left\{d_k\mid P^{res}_k(d;g)=P^{dev}_k(d_k)\right\}\\ d^N&=\arg\max_{d}\left\{\sum_{k}\pi_k(d,g^*(d))\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{9.2.2.22}g∗(d)d∗(g)dN​=arggmax​{k∑​wk​(g;d)}=argdmax​{k∑​πk​(d;g)}={dk​∣Pkres​(d;g)=Pkdev​(dk​)}=argdmax​{k∑​πk​(d,g∗(d))}​(9.2.2.22)

where d={dk}d=\{d_k\}d={dk​} and, in the second line, competitive development that takes defense as given is characterized by market clearing between the residential and developer sides. Since defense is coastal, g∗(d)g^*(d)g∗(d) is approximated on an interpolation grid over coastal development only, and coastal and inland development are solved as a fixed point. With TTT periods, commitment fixes the whole path of defense, while non-commitment is solved by backward induction on the stocks of past development and defense. The model is solved over 267 neighborhoods on a finite horizon from 2050 to 2500 with 2015 data as initial conditions; defense is chosen every 50 years and then depreciates fully, while residents move and developers build every five years.

Key Estimates

  • Demand: the rent coefficient is −0.032-0.032−0.032 (s.e. 0.004; rents in dollars per square meter per year, mean 144) and the flooding coefficient is −0.490-0.490−0.490 (s.e. 0.097; meters per year, mean 0.15); the amenity coefficient is 0.110, and the first-stage F-statistic is 108. Mean flooding is equivalent to 2.30 dollars of yearly rent per square meter, or about 320 million dollars per year over 140 million square meters of floor space, close to the 300 million of accounting damages in Budiyono et al. (2015). Raising flooding by one, two and four standard deviations (0.26 m each) implies further yearly damages of 560 million, 1.1 billion and 2.2 billion dollars.

  • Supply: the coefficient on the height term is 1.415 (s.e. 0.412) and the land-price coefficient is 0.169 (s.e. 0.039; prices in 100 dollars per square meter), with first-stage F-statistics of 13.75 and 17.80. Flooding has a small insignificant direct effect (0.063, about 6 dollars per square meter at the mean), while mean ruggedness costs 125 dollars per square meter.

Counterfactuals

Coastal outcomes are new development and defense in North Jakarta (22 percent of land area), normalized by their full-commitment values in 2050; welfare is a city-wide net present value in 2015 dollars relative to zero defense.

  • Full commitment: the first best is gradual managed retreat. Coastal development is 1.00, 0.67 and 0.30 in 2050, 2100 and 2200, defense is 1.00, 1.36 and 1.77, and welfare gains are 14.73 billion dollars.

  • No commitment: development is 1.62, 1.30 and 0.84 and defense is 1.34, 2.05 and 3.07, so new coastal development is about twice the first best in 2100 and nearly three times in 2200. Welfare is −4.66-4.66−4.66 billion: inaction dominates, and moral hazard costs nearly 20 billion dollars.

  • Partial commitment: limited commitment (commitment in 2050 only) yields 1.01 billion; delayed commitment (commitment after 2050) yields 12.30 billion, so non-commitment in 2050 alone costs 2.43 billion. With political myopia, in which governments ignore defense costs borne by their successors, the figures are −1.06-1.06−1.06 and 6.26 billion.

  • Integrated policy: inland investment that cuts coastal demand by 25 percent gives 13.77 billion with commitment and 10.04 without; slowing subsidence by 25 percent gives 22.33 and 20.46; regulation equal to 25 percent of the Pigouvian tax gives 11.15 and −0.95-0.95−0.95. Each lowers the return to forcing defense.

  • Coastal prices: with defense g(x)=xgC+(1−x)gNg(x)=xg^C+(1-x)g^Ng(x)=xgC+(1−x)gN for x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]x∈[0,1], model-implied coastal land prices match the observed 2015 prices only under low commitment, whereas flood misperceptions alone would require extreme and prolonged optimism. Moral hazard thus rationalizes the incomplete capitalization of flood risk.

  • Robustness and extensions: the full versus no commitment welfare pair is 6.21 and −2.41-2.41−2.41 for β=0.93\beta=0.93β=0.93 and 33.96 and −18.55-18.55−18.55 for β=0.97\beta=0.97β=0.97. The no-commitment outcome worsens with political lobbying (−8.69-8.69−8.69), uncertain flooding (−13.78-13.78−13.78), endogenous inland amenities (−12.56-12.56−12.56) and depreciating development (−20.02-20.02−20.02).

This is the definition of social welfare for the single flood-prone coastal location of the theory. The two arguments are the amount of coastal development ddd (buildings) and the amount of coastal defense ggg (for example the height of a sea wall). Private profits π(d,g)\pi(d,g)π(d,g) collect everything that accrues to private agents, namely the consumer surplus of residents plus the producer surplus of developers. Public costs e(d,g)e(d,g)e(d,g) collect everything paid by the government: flood-defense infrastructure and aid for flooded development. All three objects are in money units, and welfare weights private and public dollars equally (no cost of public funds).

The paper imposes only order restrictions, with no continuity or differentiability. Both π\piπ and eee increase in ddd and in ggg, and for d′>dd'>dd′>d and g′>gg'>gg′>g,

π(d′,g′)−π(d,g′)>π(d′,g)−π(d,g),e(d′,g′)−e(d,g′)<e(d′,g)−e(d,g),\begin{aligned} \pi(d',g')-\pi(d,g') &> \pi(d',g)-\pi(d,g), \\ e(d',g')-e(d,g') &< e(d',g)-e(d,g), \end{aligned}π(d′,g′)−π(d,g′)e(d′,g′)−e(d,g′)​>π(d′,g)−π(d,g),<e(d′,g)−e(d,g),​

so π\piπ has increasing differences (defense protects new buildings) and eee has decreasing differences (defense reduces the aid that new buildings require). Subtracting the second line from the first shows that www itself has increasing differences in (d,g)(d,g)(d,g): development and defense are complements for the planner as well.

The split of www into π\piπ and eee is the source of the friction. Developers care about π\piπ only, the government about www, and the gap eee is what equations (3) to (6) vary. The stylized example is the special case with binary choices: with a wall and development π=r−c=ϵ\pi=r-c=\epsilonπ=r−c=ϵ and the public cost is eee, so

w(1,1)=ϵ−e<0=w(0,0),r−e>0⏟ex post gain from the wall once c is sunk,w(1,1)=\epsilon-e<0=w(0,0),\qquad \underbrace{r-e>0}_{\text{ex post gain from the wall once } c \text{ is sunk}} ,w(1,1)=ϵ−e<0=w(0,0),ex post gain from the wall once c is sunkr−e>0​​,

which is why the wall is not built under commitment but is built without it whenever r>e>ϵr>e>\epsilonr>e>ϵ.

These are the planner's two best-response functions. d∗(g)d^*(g)d∗(g) is the welfare-maximizing development for a given level of defense, and g∗(d)g^*(d)g∗(d) is the welfare-maximizing defense for a given level of development. The first best (d^∗,g^∗)(\hat{d}^*,\hat{g}^*)(d^∗,g^​∗) is defined as a point at which both hold at once, d^∗=d∗(g^∗)\hat{d}^*=d^*(\hat{g}^*)d^∗=d∗(g^​∗) and g^∗=g∗(d^∗)\hat{g}^*=g^*(\hat{d}^*)g^​∗=g∗(d^∗), which is the paper's way of writing joint maximization of w(d,g)w(d,g)w(d,g) in equation (1) as a fixed point. Strictly speaking, a mutual best response is necessary for a joint maximum but not always sufficient (a coordinate-wise maximum need not be a global one), so the definition implicitly selects the fixed point that is the joint maximizer.

Writing the first best as a fixed point of two maps is what makes it comparable with the other regimes: equations (3), (4) and (5) keep the same structure and only change which objective each map maximizes or who moves first. Because www has increasing differences in (d,g)(d,g)(d,g), both maps are increasing: more defense justifies more development and more development justifies more defense, even for the planner.

In a smooth interior case the two conditions are the first-order conditions

πd(d,g)=ed(d,g),πg(d,g)=eg(d,g),\pi_d(d,g)=e_d(d,g),\qquad \pi_g(d,g)=e_g(d,g),πd​(d,g)=ed​(d,g),πg​(d,g)=eg​(d,g),

so the marginal private benefit of each action is equated to its marginal public cost. The regimes below break the first equality, because developers ignore ede_ded​, or alter the timing in which the second is imposed. In the note the function g∗(d)g^*(d)g∗(d) reappears as the ex post defense rule gn(d)g^n(d)gn(d) in equation (4) and gN(d)g^N(d)gN(d) in equation (5), and in the quantitative model as the first line of equation (22).

Weak commitment is a leader-follower game in which the government moves first. It cannot tax or regulate development, but it can credibly fix defense before developers build. The first object, dc(g)d^c(g)dc(g), is the reaction of competitive developers: they maximize private profits π\piπ and ignore public costs eee. The second object, g^c\hat{g}^cg^​c, is a single number, not a function: the government picks the level of defense that maximizes welfare from equation (1) along the developers' reaction curve, and the outcome for development is d^c=dc(g^c)\hat{d}^c=d^c(\hat{g}^c)d^c=dc(g^​c).

The difference from the first best in equation (2) is only in the first map, dc(g)d^c(g)dc(g) instead of d∗(g)d^*(g)d∗(g). With one instrument, ggg, the government has to do two jobs, protecting buildings and discouraging over-building, so it cannot reach the first best. In a smooth interior case the government's first-order condition is

wg(dc(g),g)+wd(dc(g),g)∂dc(g)∂g=0.w_g\left(d^c(g),g\right)+w_d\left(d^c(g),g\right)\frac{\partial d^c(g)}{\partial g}=0 .wg​(dc(g),g)+wd​(dc(g),g)∂g∂dc(g)​=0.

Since developers set πd=0\pi_d=0πd​=0, the welfare effect of extra development is wd=πd−ed=−ed<0w_d=\pi_d-e_d=-e_d<0wd​=πd​−ed​=−ed​<0, and since dcd^cdc is increasing in ggg the second term is negative. Hence wg>0w_g>0wg​>0 at the weak-commitment outcome: the government deliberately provides less defense than would be optimal ex post for the development that actually occurs, g^c<g∗(d^c)\hat{g}^c<g^*(\hat{d}^c)g^​c<g∗(d^c), in order to restrain developers.

This inequality is also the reason the regime is fragile. Once d^c\hat{d}^cd^c is sunk, the government would like to raise defense to g∗(d^c)g^*(\hat{d}^c)g∗(d^c), and if developers expect this the outcome unravels to equation (4). The ranking of this regime against the others is in equation (7).

Weak non-commitment keeps the same two objectives as equation (3) but changes the timing. The government's announcement is not believed, so defense is chosen after development is sunk and is a function of it: gn(d)g^n(d)gn(d) maximizes welfare for whatever ddd is in place, and is the same function as g∗(d)g^*(d)g∗(d) in equation (2). Developers are small, so each takes the eventual level of defense as given and dn(g)d^n(g)dn(g) maximizes private profits; it is the same function as dc(g)d^c(g)dc(g) in equation (3). The equilibrium is a fixed point, d^n=dn(g^n)\hat{d}^n=d^n(\hat{g}^n)d^n=dn(g^​n) and g^n=gn(d^n)\hat{g}^n=g^n(\hat{d}^n)g^​n=gn(d^n), that is, a Nash equilibrium between atomistic developers and an ex post optimizing government.

In a smooth interior case the two conditions are

πd(d,g)=0,πg(d,g)=eg(d,g).\pi_d(d,g)=0,\qquad \pi_g(d,g)=e_g(d,g).πd​(d,g)=0,πg​(d,g)=eg​(d,g).

Compared with the first best, the term ede_ded​ is missing from the first condition (developers do not pay for the aid or the protection their buildings will receive). Compared with weak commitment, the government no longer takes into account that its defense feeds back into development, so the restraint term wd ∂dc/∂gw_d\,\partial d^c/\partial gwd​∂dc/∂g is missing from the second.

The word weak refers to the fact that no individual developer tries to manipulate defense: each developer correctly anticipates g^n\hat{g}^ng^​n but treats it as independent of its own choice. Over-defense arises only because the government reacts to aggregate over-development. Equation (5) adds strategic manipulation by a coordinated actor. In terms of the generalized objective of equation (6), this regime is (θd,θg)=(1,0)(\theta_d,\theta_g)=(1,0)(θd​,θg​)=(1,0), and equation (7) places it between weak commitment and strong non-commitment.

Strong non-commitment reverses the leader-follower structure of equation (3): now development leads and defense follows. The second object, gN(d)g^N(d)gN(d), is the ex post welfare-maximizing defense rule, identical to gn(d)g^n(d)gn(d) in equation (4) and g∗(d)g^*(d)g∗(d) in equation (2). The first object, d^N\hat{d}^Nd^N, is a single number chosen by an actor that controls aggregate development and cares about private profits only: a current government seeking political gain, a local government that expects a national bail-out, or a developer association. This actor internalizes that more development forces more defense and uses it, and the outcome for defense is g^N=gN(d^N)\hat{g}^N=g^N(\hat{d}^N)g^​N=gN(d^N).

The second term is positive because private profits increase in defense and the defense rule increases in development. Therefore πd<0\pi_d<0πd​<0 at the optimum: aggregate development is pushed beyond the point at which it is privately profitable for given defense, because the marginal building buys additional protection for all buildings. This is the difference from equation (4), where each small developer stops at πd=0\pi_d=0πd​=0.

The regime is the mirror image of weak commitment. There, the government distorts ggg downward to pull ddd down; here, the development side distorts ddd upward to pull ggg up. It produces the largest development and defense in the ranking of equation (7), and it is the non-commitment case solved in the quantitative model as the third line of equation (22).

This is the random-utility model of residential location. The choice is static and frictionless: residents are renters, there are no moving costs, and nothing depends on where the individual lived before.

Representative utility is linear. rkr_krk​ is annual rent per square meter (dollars), fkf_kfk​ is mean flooding (meters per year), xkx_kxk​ are observed amenities and εk\varepsilon_kεk​ is an unobserved amenity common to all residents of kkk. These two lines are the Bellman equation of a landowner whose plot in location kkk already carries a building of height hhh. There are no shocks to this choice, so it is a plain maximum.

Supply of floor space is the number of built plots times floor space per plot. Consider the plots iii of location kkk at time ttt. An empty plot, dikt=0d_{ikt}=0dikt​=0, is developed with probability δkt\delta_{kt}δkt​ from equation (15). Two simplifications are implicit. Both are matters of bookkeeping that do not affect the estimation, which uses only new construction.

The cost function is built from two assumptions and one calibration. The first assumption is that the cost of each segment of the wall is proportional to its length times its total height, with a constant unit cost per meter-kilometer. The second fixes the geometry: a wall that protects against ggg meters is ggg meters high along the 60 km onshore segment, and along the 32 km offshore segment it stands 2g2g2g meters above water on top of 16 meters of water depth. The ratio two and the depth come from the planned wall, which is 4 m high onshore and 24 m high offshore, of which 8 m is above water:

offshore height=2g+16,g=4 ⟹ 2×4+16=24.\text{offshore height}=2g+16,\qquad g=4\ \Longrightarrow\ 2\times 4+16=24 .offshore height=2g+16,g=4 ⟹ 2×4+16=24.

The unit costs are backed out from the engineering estimates for the planned wall, which include maintenance equal to 35 percent of construction cost in present value. With the rounded construction figures of 2 and 6 billion dollars quoted in the paper,

2000×1.3560×4=11.25,6000×1.3532×24≈10.55\frac{2000\times 1.35}{60\times 4}=11.25,\qquad \frac{6000\times 1.35}{32\times 24}\approx 10.5560×42000×1.35​=11.25,32×246000×1.35​≈10.55

million dollars per meter-kilometer; the paper's unrounded inputs give 10.6710.6710.67 and 10.7810.7810.78. The two segments imply nearly the same unit cost despite very different heights, which supports linearity. Adding the two segments for a general ggg,

e(g)=10.67×60×g+10.78×32×(2g+16)=640.2 g+689.92 g+5519.36=5519.36+1330.12 g.\begin{aligned} e(g)&=10.67\times 60\times g+10.78\times 32\times(2g+16) \\ &=640.2\,g+689.92\,g+5519.36=5519.36+1330.12\,g . \end{aligned}e(g)​=10.67×60×g+10.78×32×(2g+16)=640.2g+689.92g+5519.36=5519.36+1330.12g.​

So there is a fixed cost of about 5.5 billion dollars for crossing the bay and a marginal cost of about 1.33 billion per meter of protection. Checking the quoted numbers:

that is, 9.5, 11 and 12 billion dollars. Because the function depends on ggg only, public costs in equation (1) do not vary with development; developers who take ggg as given then maximize the same objective as the planner, which is why the first three regimes of equation (7) coincide in the quantitative model and only strong commitment and strong non-commitment are compared in equation (22).

First line. Defense maximizes total welfare for given development. In an interior solution the marginal flood-protection benefit summed over all locations equals the marginal cost of the wall, about 1.33 billion dollars per meter by equation (21):

Second line. With defense fixed, write total private surplus as residents' gross surplus from the floor space ddd minus developers' costs. Let Pkres(d;g)P^{res}_k(d;g)Pkres​(d;g) be the inverse demand for floor space in kkk implied by equations (9) and (10), which depends on development everywhere, and let Pkdev(dk)P^{dev}_k(d_k)Pkdev​(dk​) be the supply price, the price at which developers are willing to supply dkd_kdk​ by equations (15) and (16). Then the derivative of total surplus with respect to development in one location is the gap between the two:

∂∂dk∑jπj(d;g)=Pkres(d;g)−Pkdev(dk).\frac{\partial}{\partial d_k}\sum_j\pi_j(d;g)=P^{res}_k(d;g)-P^{dev}_k(d_k).∂dk​∂​j∑​πj​(d;g)=Pkres​(d;g)−Pkdev​(dk​).

Setting it to zero for every kkk gives the market-clearing system of KKK equations in KKK unknowns in the note. This is the first welfare theorem: since eee does not depend on ddd, price-taking developers maximize total private surplus, and the competitive allocation is characterized by demand price equal to supply price in each location. It is the multi-location version of the rental-market clearing condition in equation (17).

where the second form uses the first line. Development is pushed beyond market clearing, until its supply price exceeds the demand price by the extra public spending that the marginal building triggers. This wedge is the quantitative counterpart of the term πg ∂gN/∂d\pi_g\,\partial g^N/\partial dπg​∂gN/∂d under equation (5).
